catalog_quote: Both Bilin and Awngi are tone languages while Kemant has only stress. Inadequate work on the other Agaw tongues makes it impossible to make any statement about tone elsewhere. In Bilin, tone is not truly musical. The stressed syllable has high pitch which is "often carried through to following syllables" (Tucker-Bryan 1966:500, after Palmer). Typologically this has to be classified as a tone, for such a stress may be entirely absent from non-clitic words, e.g. bəta 'dust' vs. bətá 'louse', respectively interpretable as Mid-Mid Mid-High. In Kemant, all words have stress in isolation, but some may lose it in context. ... In Awngi, Mid-Mid, High-High and Mid-High sequences are normal, while there is hardly any High-Mid sequence within one lexical morpheme. This is in harmony with the Bilin tendency to carry the High pitch of the stressed syllable over to the following syllables.

tone_statements.citation: Fallon, Paul D. 2004. The best is not good enough: Scouring a previously documented language for more. In Akinbiyi Akinlabi and Oluseye Adesola (eds.), Proceedings of the 4th World Congress of African Linguistics, New Brunswick 2003, 469-478. Köln: Rüdiger Köppe.
tone_statements.quote: Palmer (1971:89) claims that in Bilin ‘the use of tone is minimal; one syllable at the most in any word may have a high tone and in some words there is no high tone at all’. Palmer finds the term stress misleading, since ‘it is phonetically always a high pitch and it may be absent altogether from some words, even “full words”’. Appleyard (1991:19) claims that Bilin appears ‘to have maintained a full tonal accent system’. [...] In short, all descriptions of Bilin have not fully addresssed the complex behavior of Bilin prosody. Future studies will need to carefully investigate the nature of prominence (probably as pitch accent or perhaps stress)

sources.note: A state-of-documentation paper whose section 2 (p. 471) reviews every prior statement on Bilin prosody - Palmer 1971:89 'use of tone is minimal; at most one high-toned syllable per word, some words none', Palmer rejecting 'stress' because prominence is always high pitch and may be absent, Appleyard 1991:19 'full tonal accent system', Lamberti & Tonelli 1996 'not a tone language; undecidable stress- vs pitch accent' - then adds the author's own observations: many prominence patterns, some suffixes never/always prominent, antepenultimate prominence possible, contrasts (louse vs dirt) surfacing…

sources.note: Classes Bilin with Awngi as the two Agaw languages that 'appear to have a tonal accent system comparable with' Lowland East Cushitic (Somali/Afar/Oromo type: simple two-term, culminative High), in contrast to Kemant and Khamtanga which are moving to predictable stress; p. 18 repeats 'the two languages which appear to have maintained a full tonal accent system' and relates Bilin case endings to the LEC tonal Subject case. No tone count for Bilin beyond the High-accent framing.
